q0031: Sensitive data (PII, card numbers) leaving by email, USB or upload → DLP. NetFlow sees traffic volumes, not what is inside the files.
q0032: Stripping or rejecting special characters from form input = input validation (sanitization), the defense against injection attacks.
q0033: Reduce the IMPACT of a click → limit what happens after it (block execution with EDR). Reduce the CHANCE of a click → training and email filtering.
q0034: When the normal fix (patching or upgrading) is not possible, the extra safeguard you add instead is a compensating control.
q0035: Accounts built by hand keep coming out wrong → automate with a user provisioning script that applies a role template every time.
q0036: Reviewing logs finds things after they happen = detective. Stopping them = preventive; fixing afterward = corrective; discouraging = deterrent.
q0037: Cheap, cloud-based and no servers to manage = serverless (functions as a service): you pay only while the code runs.
q0038: Stop alerting on activity confirmed as benign = tuning, which cuts false positives.
q0039: Password accepted but MFA failing again and again = the password is already compromised and someone is guessing or spamming the second factor.
q0040: Natural disasters (weather, earthquakes, floods) → geographic dispersion: put redundant sites far enough apart that one event cannot hit both.
q0041: BYOD risks: jailbroken or rooted devices, side loading, and personal and corporate data mixed on one device. VM escape and buffer overflows belong elsewhere.
q0042: Is a threat worth insuring against? How often it happens (ARO) × cost per event (SLE) = ALE. MTTR, MTBF and RTO measure recovery and reliability.
q0043: Security awareness teaches users what to do: recognize phishing and report it. Tool-based detection and pen testing are not user communications.
q0046: Overwriting memory, a return address or a register = buffer overflow. Exploiting the gap between a check and a use = race condition.
q0047: A legacy system that must keep running → segmentation (restrict who can reach it). Isolation cuts it off completely; decommissioning removes it.
q0048: Data hidden inside an image, audio or video file = steganography. Encryption makes data unreadable; steganography hides that it exists at all.
q0049: Legal hold = preserve everything relevant, in every form, until the lawyers release it. No fixed end date and no deleting.
q0050: One factor of each kind: know (password, PIN), have (token, smart card, phone), are (fingerprint, face). IP addresses and locations are not 'have' factors.
q0051: A new IR plan or playbook gets tested with a tabletop exercise: a discussion-based walkthrough of a scenario, with nothing touched for real.
q0052: A legitimate site blocked under the wrong category (gambling, adult) → fix its categorization in the web content filter.
q0053: Damage done through a valid internal account points to an insider threat, whether the user acted on purpose or carelessly.
q0054: Leavers should lose access immediately. Automating deprovisioning (disabling accounts) closes the gap that manual offboarding leaves.
q0055: No internet access at all, physically separated = air gap. Logical segmentation still shares the network and can be misconfigured.
q0056: Show only the last four digits = masking. Tokenization swaps the number for a token; hashing and encryption hide all of it.
q0057: Files renamed with a new extension plus a message on every screen = ransomware (.ryk is Ryuk).
q0058: Health emergencies, 911 or other life-safety services → availability is the top priority.
q0059: Banks, hospitals and card processors audit mainly because regulations require it (regulatory compliance).
q0060: DLP rollout step one: classify the data. DLP can only protect what it can recognize as sensitive.
q0061: Central collection + correlation + alerting across many log sources = SIEM.
q0062: Decommission when a risk cannot be fixed: no more authorized updates, or it cannot meet the required encryption. Configuration problems get fixed, not retired.
